newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST-Iberian bonds to rest, ponder latest rush.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Iberian bonds to rest, ponder latest rush.

text.p: Portuguese bonds may shake off recent profit-taking and advance next week, but bonos could continue to consolidate among fears they have already factored in too much good news, analysts said.

Portuguese bonds could benefit from a possible cut in both official rates as soon as this afternoon and widen their 10-year spread under Spain, but peseta bonds are expected to be worse off in one week.
At the long end, Spanish bonds are discounting sharp inflation falls. The short end is expecting rate cuts.
But despite the difference in Iberian bond directionS, the spread is seen treading water next week. Analysts see no more than a five basis point increase from the current five basis points.
Both markets have been hit by profit-taking in recent days, and there are fears this trend could continue.

"The profit-taking we had in the last two days could continue ahead of the February Federal Reserve Federal Open Market Committee (meeting). I expect a volatile Spanish market, and a higher spread," said Giovanni Polastri, economist with 4CAST in London.
The FOMC will meet on February 4 and 5 and there are worries the Fed could raise rates.

Polastri expects the 10-year spread between Spain and Germany to widen toward 100 points from the current level of around 95 basis points. The spread dipped to an all-time record low at 83 bps on Wednesday.
At around 0850 GMT on Friday the long term future contract was trading at 113.42, down 46 basis points from yesterday. And only few days ago this contract was defying the level of 115.
Spanish yields also slipped beneath those of the U.S. for the first time ever and are now back over parity.
"It was weird seeing Spanish yields trading below U.S. notes'," said Alfredo Urrutia at Societe Generale in Madrid. "That triggered a profit-taking wave".
But the current consolidation should prove short-lived as the short-end of the Iberian curves still offers good value, analysts added.
"This is only going to be a consolidation, not a change in the market cycle," said Luca Jellinek at Paribas in London, who was expecting the bullish mood to resume quite soon.
As early as this afternoon, the Bank of Portugal could offer the best evidence that the interest rate decline is not over.

"I expect the central bank to cut both official rates today. They could shave the repo rate by 30 basis points to 5.9 pct, and the absorption rate by 10 bps to 6.40," said Isabel Cabral, analyst at Fincor in Lisbon.
And an official rate cut, or even the expectation of forthcoming cuts, should give a comparative advantage to Portuguese long debt overs its Spanish counterpart.
"I'm giving a 40 percent chance to cuts in rates today," said Mario Vigario, trader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon.
But he was betting anyway on the spread to Bonos widening to minus ten from the current minus five within a week.
But the best value in peripherals remains in the short end, analysts said, although they were ruling out significant changes in the next few trading days.
"I guess the Spanish yield curve can steepen a bit this week, let's say by around five basis points," Jellinek said.
The two- to ten-year bond spread in Spain was trading on Friday morning at around 146 basis points.
"I think this is fair value. It's in between 150 bps where it was before the Bank of Spain had cut its rate (on January 16) and 131 basis points where it dipped thereafter," said Urrutia.
And the same should happen in Portugal's market.

"I forecast the Portuguese yield curve will steepen from the current 75 basis points to around 100 basis points by the end of 1997. But I guess it will move only a bit in a week's time. It could steepen a little at the expense of the longer end," said Vigario.
But even in the short end, Spain is seen losing ground versus its European fellows.
In a note to clients, the Bank of America in Madrid suggested staying short of Spain and long of Italian notes in the two-year segment.

"While Spanish short-term interest rates are already discounting very sharp cuts by the Bank of Spain this year, this is not the case in Italy," explained Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
